text:
Useful, informative eye-opener & easy to read, even though written for British readership: 

These poisonous lies about Zionism need to die

Israel is a multiethnic democracy and the Jewish connection to the Holy Land reaches back millennia
Adam LeBor 

Walking along the Pilgrimage Road from the Pool of Siloam to the base of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem is a kind of time travel. Built around 2,000 years ago, its precisely engineered stone paving has recently been restored and the road opened to the public. Roman legionnaires ran amok here in 70AD, burning the shops and houses and slaughtering the Jewish rebels. A layer of ash is still embedded in the walls.

If only it were possible for Israel to arrange a trip for Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens – and for the 1,022 party members who voted for a motion (which Polanski didn’t turn up to vote for) declaring that Zionism supports an “ethnonationalist Jewish state” based on the “exclusion and/or domination” of non-Jews, while Israel must effectively be replaced by a “democratic Palestinian state”. The lie that Zionism is racism has long outlived its Soviet creators. Zionism is the movement to establish a democratic, non-exclusive Jewish state in the historic homeland of the Jewish people.

Do the Greens know that 21 per cent of Israel’s 10.3 million population are Muslim, Christian and Druze Arabs? These minorities in Israel are diplomats, judges on the supreme court, members of the Knesset, military officers, doctors, lawyers, businessmen and women, part of a thriving professional middle class. Sometimes they suffer discrimination. Modern Israel, like every democracy, is a work in progress. But the overwhelming majority of Israeli-Arabs would live nowhere else.

Nor is Zionism a “settler-colonial” ideology. In truth, the Jewish connection to Israel reaches back millennia to the time of Abraham. Jewish kings and dynasties exercised centuries of intermittent sovereignty from the Davidic era, around 3,000 years ago, until 70AD. Even after Titus’s soldiers destroyed the Temple the Jews rose again against the Romans, in 132AD, before being exiled. The Jewish connection to the Holy Land continued through religious and spiritual Zionism.

The father of modern Zionism was Theodor Herzl, an Austro-Hungarian journalist and the author of The Jewish State, published in 1896. Herzl argued that, despite the new legal protections given to Jews by modern European states, deep-rooted anti-Semitism meant they had no future in Europe. He was correct, as later events proved.

Modern Zionism was not an outlier, but one of many modern anti-colonial movements pressuring the creaking Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian empires to grant freedom to their subject peoples. Another was the emergence of Arab, and later, Palestinian nationalism – the latter partly as a response to Zionism. Palestinian leaders then – unlike their counterparts nowadays – acknowledged the historic Jewish connection to the Holy Land, although they completely rejected the idea of Jewish sovereignty.

Zionism, like socialism, has many currents. Some Zionists even believe in a bi-national Jewish-Arab state. Nowadays a minority of extremists want to see the Palestinians expelled and Biblical-style Jewish sovereignty restored. Neither of them is intrinsic to the ideology. Tony Blair and Josef Stalin were both socialists, but otherwise had nothing in common. 

Interviewed by the BBC, Polanski sought to square the circle. The motion would stand for two years, he said, although ultimately he would like to amend it. “I want to move away from one state, towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide their future for themselves.” Israelis and Palestinians have decided their own futures for decades.

In November 1947, the UN passed Resolution 181. It proposed dividing Palestine, then under British rule, into independent Jewish and Arab states, linked through economic union. The Yishuv, the Zionist leadership, accepted it. The Palestinians did not. The previous month Abdul Rahman Hassan Azzam Pasha, secretary-general of the Arab League, had declared that a Jewish state would lead to “a war of extermination and momentous massacre which will be spoken of like the Mongolian massacre and the Crusades”.

In May 1948, five Arab armies invaded. There was no war of extermination. Instead Israel, fighting for its life, won. Around 700,000 Palestinians fled, an event known as “the Nakba”, or catastrophe. The picture is complex. Some departed before the war, some were encouraged to leave by Arab leaders and some were expelled by Israeli troops. Many simply took flight in the terror and chaos.

In Jaffa, the Arab mayor, Yousef Heikal, encouraged his fellow Arabs to leave – much of the middle class had already departed months earlier. In Haifa, the Jewish mayor, Shabtai Levy, pleaded with local Arabs not to leave. Wars and collapsing empires – and their aftermath – have produced misery and refugees for millennia.

The case of Israel/Palestine is not unique. The numbers involved are a fraction of the catastrophic consequences of, for example, the 1947 partition of India and Pakistan: millions were displaced amid widespread massacres and mass rape. Across eastern Europe, millions of ethnic Germans were expelled or fled after 1945.

The 1923 Treaty of Lausanne ordered the transfer of more than one million ethnic Greeks from their centuries-old homeland in what became the new Turkish state, and the expulsion of hundreds of thousands of Muslims from Greece to Turkey. There is no talk among Greens of the “ethnonationalist” Greek or Turkish states, even though they were specifically created as such by an international treaty.

In July 1995, the Bosnian Serb army committed genocide at Srebrenica, murdering more than 8,300 Muslim men and boys. The Bosnian Serb entity remains a recognised, functioning part of Bosnia Herzegovina, ignored by the progressive gaze.

The early 1990s Oslo Accords gave the Palestinians limited self-government. In response Yassir Arafat launched the Second Intifada of suicide bombings. A series of negotiations followed in the early 2000s under American leadership which broadly offered the Palestinians around 95 per cent of the West Bank. The Palestinians rejected every proposal.

In 2025 Israel withdrew from Gaza. The following year the Hamas terrorist movement won legislative elections in the West Bank and Gaza. There it set up a quasi-Palestinian state. Billions of dollars of aid was channelled into building up an army and tunnel network hundreds of miles long. On October 7 2023, Hamas carried out the worst mass slaughter of Jews since the Holocaust, and killed any likelihood of a Palestinian state.

Offered numerous opportunities for peace and statehood, the Palestinians have refused every one. Instead they – and Hamas – have been rewarded by western countries, including the UK, with recognition of a ghost state that does not exist.

Earlier this month, Mahmoud Abbas, the 90-year-old president of the Palestinian Authority, postponed elections again – this time until 2027. There have been none since 2006. Perhaps one day the Palestinians will be given the opportunity to vote for a leadership that wants to live alongside Israel in peace and security – and the Greens will reconnect with reality.

text:
Annavaram Devasthanam offers a deeply fulfilling pilgrimage experience, especially when paired with the right stay and planning. Based on a recent family visit, here is a comprehensive review and guide for anyone planning a trip to the temple town.

Accommodation: 

Shiva Sadan & Vishnu Sadan
Staying overnight on the hill or near the temple complex provides a peaceful atmosphere.

 Room Rate: ₹1,500 per night for a family accommodation.

 Facilities: The rooms in Shiva Sadan (and similarly Vishnu Sadan) are exceptionally spacious, well-ventilated, and fully equipped with air conditioning, water geysers, and all essential modern amenities for a comfortable stay.

 Commuting Tip: These guest houses are situated at a slight distance from the main temple location. Having a private vehicle or arranging local transport makes getting around much easier, especially with family.

Darshan Options & Temple Access
Lord Satyanarayana Swamy's darshan and temple visits are smooth and accessible, with multiple tiers depending on your preference and budget:

 Special Darshan (₹200): Grants entry into the inner sanctum of the temple for a closer, more personal experience.

Food & Dining Insights

 Lunch: Free meals are provided for pilgrims during lunchtime as part of the Devasthanam's traditional service.

 Dinner & Snacks: Options for dinner on the hill are limited. Furthermore, due to fluctuating crowds, private tiffin and tea stalls can be sparse, with local eateries offering standard, average fare. It is wise to plan evening meals ahead, potentially exploring options down in the town at the foot of the hill.

டல்லாஸ்–ஃபோர்ட் வொர்த் பகுதியில் அமைந்துள்ள DFW இந்து ஆலயம் ஏக்தா மந்திர் சென்று, இன்று நடைபெற்ற மகா ஆரத்தியில பங்கேற்று இறைவனை வழிபட்டது மிகுந்த மனநிறைவையும் மகிழ்ச்சியையும் அளித்தது. 

ஆலயத்தின் தலைவர் திருமதி மகாலட்சுமி சிவகுமார் அவர்கள், தலைவர் குழுத் தலைவர் திரு. கேம்சந்த் நங்க்ரானி அவர்கள் மற்றும் நிர்வாகக் குழு உறுப்பினர்கள் அன்புடன் வரவேற்று, ஆலயத்தின் சிறப்புகளை எடுத்துரைத்தனர். அவர்களுக்கு எனது மனமார்ந்த நன்றிகளைத் தெரிவித்துக் கொள்கிறேன்.

“ஒற்றுமையே வலிமை” என்ற உயரிய தத்துவத்தைப் பிரதிபலிக்கும் ஏக்தா மந்திரில், விநாயகர், மகாலட்சுமி, வெங்கடேசப் பெருமாள், சிவபெருமான் – பார்வதி தேவி, ஸ்ரீ ராமர், சீதாதேவி, லட்சுமணர், அனுமன், ராதா கிருஷ்ணர், ஐயப்பன், துர்கை அம்மன் உள்ளிட்ட பல்வேறு தெய்வங்களின் சந்நிதிகள் ஒரே இடத்தில் அமைந்திருப்பது நமது பாரதத்தின் ஆன்மிக ஒற்றுமையையும், வளமான பண்பாட்டுப் பாரம்பரியத்தையும் பறைசாற்றுகிறது.

இந்த நிகழ்வை சிறப்பாக ஏற்பாடு செய்த தமிழக பாஜகவின் NRI பிரிவு மாநில அமைப்பாளர் திரு சுந்தர் அவர்கள் மற்றும் அவரது அணியினருக்கு என் மனமார்ந்த வாழ்த்துக்களை தெரிவித்துக் கொள்கிறேன்.

text:
Bazaar diplomacy will bury American supremacy

Today, America needs the world. It needs Russian diesel to calm its pumps, Chinese goodwill to steady its markets, Indian capital to build its refineries and Indian talent to run its industries.

“Power always thinks it has a great soul and vast views beyond the comprehension of the weak,” John Adams wrote to Thomas Jefferson two centuries ago. The second President of the US understood what Donald Trump, the 47th, refuses to learn. Power acquired at any price eventually bankrupts the buyer. Last week, Mumbai, emerging India’s corporate abode staged a vivid, almost vaudevillian demonstration of that bitter truth.

On Tuesday last, Secretary of State Marco Rubio with his wife and Ambassador Sergio Gor in tow landed in Mumbai. The ambience was awesome and the symbolism scandalous. Soon after their arrival, America’s 250th birthday was hosted and toasted at the Jio World Convention Centre in Bandra Kurla Complex, built by the very business tycoon Washington had come to court.

Next morning, the most powerful diplomat of the most powerful nation was keeping appointments like a salesman making a sales pitch. He along with Gor met both Gautam Adani and Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran before he began other official meetings. Neither side said a word about what was discussed.

The irony was impossible to ignore. Adani has spent two years battling an American lawsuit that almost dented his group’s global ambitions. The Tatas, whose flagship TCS developed business for American clients, watched Trump slap a punishing fee on H-1B visas that made sending Indian techies to manage those very clients prohibitively painful. The persons Trumpian establishment wounded were now being wooed by Washington. Few scripts are written with such sardonic symmetry.

And now comes the pilgrimage to Jamnagar. Gor, an envoy who strolls like a lord through Delhi’s corridors of power, had to accompany his boss across Gujarat to seek an audience with Mukesh Ambani and his son Anant. The mission was pure commerce. Both pleaded with Ambani to process Venezuelan crude, invest in America and finally facilitate the President’s refinery dreams in Texas come true.

The Ambanis, masters of message and image, orchestrated the optics with surgical skill. First came pictures of Rubio and Gor with the younger Ambanis, the patriarch pointedly absent, followed after an hour later by a frame of four before the family temple. Finally, a photograph of three of them—Rubio, Gor and Mukesh—lounging casually in a room wrapped in greenery. It was a cruel joke choreographed in pixels.

Three Indian business houses with a combined market value below a trillion dollars were setting the terms of trade for a nation with a GDP of over $30 trillion.

Equally symbolic was who stayed away from the highly-hyped event. Most of the titans who granted private audience were conspicuous by their absence at the anniversary celebration itself. The only diplomatically correct gesture came from the Indian government. External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar attended with the Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri and obliged his hosts with a bilateral meeting.

Yet Jaishankar delivered his discomfort with diplomatic deftness. He raised the champagne flute for the toast and placed it back on the table without a sip. Then he told Rubio, in good humour but with unmistakable sarcasm, “You won’t be counted as a friend of India until you really understand cricket,” before reminding both Indian and American guests that Saurabh Netravalkar, America’s leading cricketer, hails from Mumbai.

The message was elegant and exact. India plays both one-dayers and Test matches, Trump just plays T20.

But Rubio had nothing concrete to offer India. He repeated the familiar refrain that a trade deal with India was all but done. What India received is a temporary reprieve from punitive tariffs over Russian oil, a favour as fragile as the mood of the man who granted it. And that mood swings wildly. For years, Trump painted China as a predatory menace plundering American wealth. In September, he rolled out not one but two red carpets for Xi Jinping—greeted him on the tarmac at Andrews air base, gave him a guided tour of the National Archives and hosted a lavish State dinner. The Trump-Xi summit produced pageantry and pandas, but precious little policy.

On Russia, the reversal is even more ridiculous. The same Washington administration that punished India with a 25 percent penalty for buying Russian oil has now waived sanctions on Moscow and struck a deal for Russian diesel. When the US and Israel went to war with Iran in February, American diesel prices soared nearly 80 percent. Farmers fumed, truckers grumbled and a President facing voters suddenly discovered the virtues of Vladimir Putin’s oil fields. What was a crime for India became commerce for the US. Like an avaricious business leader, Trump betrayed even Ukraine by striking a deal with Russia.

Trump demanded that Kyiv stop striking Russian refineries. He advised Ukrainians to find a new leader through elections and nudged Zelenskyy towards surrendering land seized by Russian military. The defender of democracy demanded elections only from the democracy under attack.

Europe is the worst victim of Trumpian tantrums. Allies of eight decades are treated as foes by him, while he flirts with autocrats as friends. Israel, once the cornerstone of his Middle East policy, watched its Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fly in for the UN General Assembly and leave within hours, denied a White House welcome.

Iran, bombed in February, is now an interlocutor to be invited for talks whenever oil markets tremble. India was labelled a tariff abuser in one season and serenaded as a strategic partner in the next. The thread tying together these twists is not strategy but survival. Americans vote on November 3. Losing the House would paralyse the administration for the remaining two years. For Trump’s transactional architecture, conviction is a matter of convenience and principle a bargaining chip.

For more than 18 months, the world order has been battered into being a bazaar where loyalty is rented and alliances auctioned. The world may have to suffer two more years of these hysterics. For eight decades, the world needed America. That compulsion gave Washington its unmatched leverage. Mumbai this week revealed a reversal of roles that should alarm every American patriot.

Today, America needs the world. It needs Russian diesel to calm its pumps, Chinese goodwill to steady its markets, Indian capital to build its refineries and Indian talent to run its industries. A nation that once dispensed favours now solicits them. History offers a sobering lesson—if Trump fails to correct course, the next chapter of American history will be written not in Washington, but in the capitals that would have learned to live without it.

text:
Japan’s Forgotten Cosmic Breath — The Mystery of A–Un

阿吽の真理 — The Sacred Beginning and End of Existence

At Japanese temple gates stand two guardians, 金剛力士 (Kongōrikishi). One opens his mouth: 阿 (A). The other closes it: 吽 (Un).

Together they embody 阿吽 (A–Un), the beginning and culmination of existence.

These are not decorative expressions. They preserve Sanskrit अक्षर (Akṣara)—the sacred syllable as a gateway to reality.

Kūkai (空海), in 吽字義 (Unji Gi), reveals that हूँ (Hūṃ) contains four interpretive elements: Ha–A–Ū–Ma. Through them, he investigates causation, non-arising, dissolution and the illusion of independent selfhood.

ACE offers a deeper comparative investigation.

START — अ (A): The Śiva-consciousness field, within which manifestation becomes possible.

TRANSITION — ह (Ha): Threshold and transformation; ऊ (Ū) modulates the unfolding field.

END — म (Ma): Ākāśa and Nivṛtti within ACE’s operator system, returning differentiated activity toward closure.

Throughout, Śiva Conciseness remains the irreducible invariant—not identical to Buddhist emptiness, but a distinct principle for philosophical comparison.

This is not merely sound travelling through the mouth. It is an investigation into how manifestation emerges, differentiates and resolves.

Japan’s sacred architecture once made this teaching visible before anyone entered a temple.

Yet what happens when 阿吽 becomes ornament, 真言 (Shingon) becomes mechanical recitation, and 悟り (Satori) becomes a cultural expression rather than lived realization?

Japan has preserved the guardians. Has it preserved the understanding of what they guard?

The deeper spiritual loss is forgetting that the threshold to awakening lies within consciousness itself.

始まりと終わりは、真理の中にある。

Beginning and ending belong to a deeper reality.

text:
# The Book of Enoch and the Mystery of the 200 Watchers

One of the most remarkable narratives in ancient Jewish literature begins with 200 heavenly beings descending to Earth.

According to 1 Enoch, chapter 6, these beings gathered on Mount Hermon and made a binding oath.

Their leader is named Semyaza.

The Watchers took human wives, and their unions produced giants who brought violence and destruction upon the world.

But the story goes further.

In chapter 8, certain Watchers are accused of teaching humanity dangerous arts, including weaponmaking, enchantments, and celestial interpretation.

The consequences are devastating.

The Earth becomes filled with violence, and the cries of humanity rise to heaven.

God then commands judgment against the rebellious Watchers.

**Why this story matters**

The narrative explores the relationship between knowledge, power, corruption, and divine judgment.

For ancient readers, the story offered an explanation for the spread of evil before the Flood.

Today, scholars study it as an important part of Second Temple Jewish literature.

Whether interpreted as religious history, symbolism, or ancient mythology, the account remains one of the most extraordinary sections of 1 Enoch.

**The question remains: Why did ancient writers connect forbidden knowledge with the downfall of humanity?

text:
A Daily Dose of Talmud
Daf Yomi for Everyone, from My Jewish Learning

Bekhorot 36
Read the page on Sefaria
Dr. Sara Ronis
Today’s daf offers us a peek into the fascinating social dynamics of the rabbinic community.   Rabbi Tzadok had a firstborn animal. He placed barley in baskets for it, and while it was eating, its lip split.  He came before Rabbi Yehoshua. Rabbi Tzadok said to him: “Didn’t we differentiate between one who is a haver (a member of the rabbinic movement) and one who is an am ha’aretz (i.e., not a member of the rabbinic movement)?” Rabbi Yehoshua said to him: “Yes.”  Our story is set during the first century, when the Temple still stood. From the context of the Talmud’s broader discussion, it appears that Rabbi Tzadok was himself a priest. Apparently, his feed baskets had sharp edges, and the bekhor developed a blemish while eating its fodder. Rabbi Tzadok was worried he would be suspected of causing the blemish intentionally, but Rabbi Yehoshua assures him that the rabbis differentiate between one who is trusted to know the rabbinic interpretations of the law, and one who isn’t. As a haver, a member of the rabbinic guild, Rabbi Tzadok is trusted.  And because he is trusted, the blemish is considered accidental — which means the animal can be slaughtered and eaten.   But Rabbi Tzadok, who was known for being fastidious, doesn’t accept the win. Instead, he seeks a second opinion.   Rabbi Tzadok then came before Rabban Gamliel. Rabbi Tzadok said to him: “Didn’t we differentiate between a priest who is a haverand a priest who is an am ha’aretz?” Rabban Gamliel said to him: “No.” He said to him: “But Rabbi Yehoshua told me we do!”  While Rabbi Yehoshua said that we distinguish between rabbis and non-rabbis when assuming intent about blemishing a bekhor, Rabban Gamliel, head of the rabbinic community, insists that we don’t. According to him, Rabbi Tzadok would be suspected of intentionally injuring his animal. Now Rabbi Tzadok has found a more stringent position, but he has also explicitly put two colleagues — who have a famously challenging relationship — at odds.  In other stories in the Talmud, when Rabbi Yehoshua rules against Rabban Gamliel, the latter usually calls the former to the study house for a confrontation where he intimidates and humiliates him. This rarely goes well for either party. And indeed, this is what happens next on today’s daf:  Rabban Gamliel said to Rabbi Tzadok: Wait until the masters of the shields enter the study hall.   Rashi explains that the “masters of the shields” are the sages, “who fight in the war of Torah.” The martial metaphor points to the often-fraught nature of rabbinic dispute. But wait, because it’s about to get even more fraught.  When they entered the study hall, the questioner stood and asked: “Didn’t we differentiate between a haver and a priest who is an am ha’aretz?” Rabbi Yehoshua said to him: “No.” Rabban Gamliel said to him: “But they said to me in your name yes.”  Here, as in other similar stories about these two, when confronted by Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Yehoshua changes his answer to match that of his senior colleague. But, just as we find in other similar stories, Rabban Gamliel continues to force the issue.  Rabban Gamliel continued: “Yehoshua, stand on your feet and they will testify against you.”Rabbi Yehoshua stood on his feet and said: “How should I act? If I were alive and Rabbi Tzadok were dead, the living can contradict the dead. Now that I am alive and he is alive, how can the living contradict the living?”

text:
What is the "fair" merger ratio for Tesla & SpaceX?

1.
I have NO IDEA what I am talking about.

2.
The "fair" ratio is educated guesswork, not science. Both Tesla and SpaceX have massive levers that could swing either company's value dramatically. Uncertainty is high.

I've modeled Tesla & SpaceX over 20 years (Patreon subs can see the "fair" merger ratio from the full model).

3.
My model says SpaceX is the more valuable of the two. I would take a much higher SpaceX ratio than I think most Tesla investors would accept. 

So what I think is "fair" vs what would actually NEED to be offered are two different things.

Change just a few assumptions in my 20-year model and the "fair" ratio can shift meaningfully in either direction. That's how uncertain this is.

My guess (remember, I do NOT KNOW WHAT I AM TALKING ABOUT) is we land at 50/50. That would, as I write this, be a big premium for Tesla (approx 35% vs current, and approx $500/share).

The reason for this 50/50 guess is less retarded than you might think. Splitting them down the middle looks like a cheap shortcut, but it can be justified when your model can easily swing the "fair" value of either entity by 10% or more in either direction, which is absolutely the case for mine. Tweak a few assumptions and I can land at 70/30, 60/40, 55/45, 45/55, 40/60, whatever.

Then you still have to figure out how much extra value each company actually gains through unification. And I'm not talking the usual retard-in-a-suit "conglomerate discount" bullshit. I mean real, tangible value from shared assets, data, talent, supply chain, bulk buying, shared facilities, operational efficiency, faster execution etc. What is the net benefit to the new combined entity? Another 5%? 10%?

We now have a margin of error of what? 25%? 35%?
Bottom line, 50/50 is the overlap between all possible variations.

4.
Don't forget: I HAVE NO IDEA WHAT I AM TALKING ABOUT.

5.
None of us do.

Those interested can see my full valuation model here (investor level and above), including the current estimated fair merger ratio (calculated automatically from the assumptions for each line of business at both Tesla and SpaceX) plus some modeling of merger synergies:

https://t.co/3k4XAvMSgY

Better yet, build your own model. Figure out what you think the fair ratio would be, then be honest about your degree of uncertainty and how wide a band that puts around your number.

Also remember that you are retarded, and I am retarded and we have not built reusable rockets, or developed FSD etc.

INSIGHT: A drone can be shot down and still consume a costly missile. The Pentagon’s 19th October framework with BAE aims to help reduce that cost through purchases of up to 25,000 rocket-guidance kits a year.

APKWS adds laser guidance to existing 70mm rockets, turning them into precision weapons capable of engaging drones. A laser marks the target and the guidance kit steers the rocket toward it. US Air Forces Central documented F-16s carrying these rockets in the region in June 2025.

Where these rockets can do the job, they offer a way to conserve more expensive air-to-air missiles for threats that require them. Successful interception and sustainable ammunition supply are separate problems.

BAE already advertises capacity for at least 25,000 kits annually. The new framework covers up to 7 years of procurement, with a path to expand capacity to 35,000 a year as allied demand materializes.

Those are planned quantities. Congress still has to authorize and fund the procurement, and BAE says the multiyear contract is still being negotiated.

text:
Good morning you lovely lot.

IT’S SUNDAY! THE HOLIEST DAY OF THE YORKSHIRE CALENDAR! 😂

Firstly, I hope you’re all safe and haven’t suffered too much damage from the storm.

My lads have been working out in it, and by all accounts, the conditions were absolutely biblical.

Horizontal rain, howling winds and enough water falling from the sky to make Noah start checking the warranty on his ark.

I very nearly felt sorry for them.

Nearly.

But then I remembered I’m management, and apparently we’re not allowed to show weakness. 🤣🤣

Seriously though, they’ve done a cracking job in some horrendous conditions, and I’m proud of every one of them.

Meanwhile, I’m still suffering slightly from jet lag after Florida.

Just as my body was beginning to understand what country it was in, somebody decided to throw the clocks going back into the equation.

Brilliant.

My body clock is now so confused it doesn’t know whether to sleep, eat breakfast or order a margarita.

I’ve been awake at ridiculous hours, falling asleep when I shouldn’t and generally wandering around like a Victorian ghost with a caffeine addiction.

And now we’ve gained an extra hour in bed.

Wonderful, except nobody bothered to inform my brain, which apparently operates on Florida time, railway time and whatever time the bloody cat thinks it is.

I haven’t even got a cat. That’s how confused I am. 🤦🏻‍♂️🤣

BUT ENOUGH OF THAT. TODAY IS YORKSHIRE PUDDING DAY! 🎉

Forget the traditional interpretation of Sunday as a holy day.

In Yorkshire, we worship at the altar of the roasting tin.

And today, once again, I shall be accepting photographic submissions of your finest Yorkshire puddings.

PHOTO ENTRIES MUST BE IN BY 14:00.

The grand draw for the best entry will take place at 16:00.

I’ll be judging height, colour, structural integrity and, most importantly, whether the thing could hold enough gravy to float a small fishing vessel.

Flat puddings will be treated with suspicion.

Burnt offerings will be referred to the appropriate authorities.

And anyone submitting a photograph of Aunt Bessie’s frozen puddings will be immediately disqualified and possibly reported to the Yorkshire authorities.

THIS IS YORKSHIRE, NOT A CRIME SCENE IN THE FREEZER AISLE! 🤣🤣

A LITTLE YORKSHIRE HISTORY!

On this day in 1854, the famous Charge of the Light Brigade took place during the Crimean War.

And there’s a Yorkshire connection!

The charge was led by Lord Cardigan, whose family owned vast areas of Leeds. Two Leeds men, Charles Macaulay of Woodhouse and James Barrass of Holbeck, took part and survived.

Hundreds of cavalrymen charged straight towards Russian artillery following a disastrously confused order.

An extraordinary display of bravery in the face of catastrophic military leadership.

A bit like being told by management that everything’s going to plan when you can clearly see the whole thing’s gone tits up! 🤣

And finally, be kind.

Behind every smile there might be somebody struggling, worrying or simply trying to get through another difficult day.

It costs nothing to show a little patience, offer a kind word or check in on someone.

Always try to be nice, but never fail to be kind.

Right then, it’s Sunday. You’ve got puddings to make, photographs to submit and a Yorkshireman to impress.

Remember: 14:00 deadline, 16:00 draw.

And if you’re using Aunt Bessie’s, don’t bother trying to disguise them. I know what a factory-produced pudding looks like. 😂

Have a cracking Sunday, folks.

May your puddings rise, your gravy flow and your roast potatoes be crispy!

Laugh hard. Run fast. Be kind. ♥️

text:
AI Sovereignty, Now Available in Two Vendor-Locked Editions

The AI race has acquired blocs, membership rules and the diplomatic charm of a protection racket with better slide decks.

The Associated Press reports that countries are being pressed toward two competing systems. The U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative offers access to advanced chips, technology partnerships, high-tech manufacturing and “trusted” supply chains. China’s World AI Cooperation Organization offers a more inclusive pitch built around cooperation, affordability and open-source AI. [1]

Kazakhstan decided to order from both menus.

Its government formally joined Pax Silica on June 25. Roughly three weeks later, it became a founding member of China’s AI organization alongside 28 other countries, including Pakistan and Russia. Kazakhstan has critical minerals, cheap electricity and ambitions to build a data-center economy. It also has the awkward geography of a country that cannot afford ideological purity from either direction. [1][2]

That makes it an unusually honest preview of what “AI sovereignty” is starting to mean.

The stack is foreign policy now

This is not only a contest over chatbots. The package includes chips, power, cloud capacity, data centers, manufacturing, critical minerals, standards and access to the most capable models. [1][2]

Kazakhstan’s own Pax Silica announcement described the arrangement as a route into AI infrastructure, semiconductor supply chains, energy storage, advanced manufacturing and trusted models. NVIDIA separately described plans to expand computing infrastructure in the country, including new GPU deployments. [2][4]

China’s pitch comes with different language. Its foreign ministry says the World AI Cooperation Organization is meant to narrow the global AI divide and help the Global South build capacity. Chinese models are often cheaper and more open than the American frontier systems, which makes the offer attractive to countries that cannot spend their way into an independent stack. [1][3]

Both sales pitches contain real benefits. Both also arrive with dependencies attached.

AP reports that the State Department says countries cannot be trusted members of Pax Silica while substantively supporting a competing vision for advanced AI. Beijing calls its own initiative open and inclusive, but it is also building influence through standards, infrastructure and technology that other governments will rely on. [1][3]

One club has the best chips. The other promises a cheaper cover charge. The fine print on both starts with: your sovereign stack will be built with somebody else’s machinery.

Everyone is hedging until the bill arrives

Kazakhstan is not alone. Indonesia joined China’s organization while trying to draw investment from both sides. Singapore is taking American AI investment while considering China’s group. Saudi Arabia has deals involving advanced U.S. chips and a platform built on a Chinese open model. Kyoto professor Takahiro Tsuchiya told AP that Japan is aligned with Washington on strategic technology but is unlikely to reject cheaper Chinese models for lower-risk uses; that is his assessment, not an announced Japanese government policy. [1]

France is trying to preserve another route through Mistral. Carnegie analysts cited by AP assess that Britain and Germany, despite their economic and military weight, lack a frontier-model ecosystem that would free them from reliance on American chips and data-center deals. [1]

None of this proves that every partnership becomes an exclusive political alliance. Countries can and will mix suppliers where the contracts, risks and diplomatic pressure permit it. Kazakhstan’s dual membership is evidence that hedging remains possible today.

The pressure described by AP is about whether that space stays open. Once a country builds government systems, industrial capacity, energy projects and security rules around one technology stack, switching becomes expensive. Standards harden. Talent follows the money. Dependence becomes architecture.

Then the diplomatic choice has already been made, one data center at a time.

Sovereignty with terms of service

Washington and Beijing are selling different versions of AI power. The United States has the strongest frontier chips and corporate ecosystem. China can offer affordable models, infrastructure and a political message tailored to countries tired of being told that access is reserved for the trusted. [1]

Smaller countries are not confused. They see the bargain clearly enough to want both.

The question is how long the two superpowers will tolerate that answer. If the AI economy splits into rival supply chains, sovereignty may come down to choosing which capital, cloud and standards system a government can least afford to lose.

A flag over the data center does not settle who controls the stack beneath it.

Can smaller countries keep one foot in each AI bloc, or will infrastructure dependence eventually force a political choice?

Sources:
[1] Associated Press: Why some countries struggle to pick sides in the U.S.-China AI race — October 25, 2026

I’ve been watching the Brooklyn Nets' first two games closely—as I firmly believe they’ll be the surprise team this season—and I’ve reached a few (very early) conclusions: 

Egor Demin is the real deal. He managed to find his rhythm in the fourth quarter against the Cavs, bouncing back from a poor preseason and a dreadful first game. I have high hopes for this kid. 

Mikel Brown Jr. has a bright future ahead of him. 

Moe Wagner shouldn’t be getting this many minutes; he’s too slow and offers nothing on the defensive end. 

Chaney Johnson is seeing a lot of playing time—and while he’s an intriguing prospect, the fact that he’s getting so many minutes suggests the free-agent market was quite weak. 

The Randle-MPJ duo is as potent offensively as it is liability-prone defensively. 

I don’t think MPJ will be in Brooklyn for much longer. I suspect they’ll trade him for a player who’s a better fit for Jordi’s system. A long-shot scenario would be a trade for Deni Avdija; I get the feeling Portland won’t look to re-sign him, which could open a door for Brooklyn—even if it means overpaying to get the deal done. 

The 2025 draft class is a bit concerning. Traore didn’t get off to a great start; I’d like to see more of Saraf, who contributes more defensively, even if he’s still quite raw on the offensive end. Wolf can provide some offense, but his minutes will ultimately depend on his ability to defend.

0-2—plenty of room for improvement, but it’s still very early days.

text:
Remembering Vincent Price, who died on this day in 1993. 
Price was a legendary American actor, who began his career as a leading man, but found international fame in the horror genre. Yet he was adept at comedy and conventional drama, and should not be remembered as a one trick ghoul dripping blood. Price was a polymath of exceptional intelligence, and a man of wit, generosity and charm. He was born on May 27, 1911, in Missouri. In 1933, he graduated with a degree in English and a minor in art history from Yale. He made his film debut in “Service de Luxe” (1938), and was memorable as Gene Tierney’s delectably amusing boyfriend in the film noir “Laura” (1944). He reunited with Tierney in “Leave Her to Heaven” (1945), and “Dragonwyck” (1946), in which he portrayed the dashing but sinister man she marries. He also appeared in a series of film noirs including “The Bribe” (1949), with Robert Taylor and Ava Gardner. Price excelled in comedic parts when given the chance. Portraying a ham actor in “His Kind of Woman” (1951), with Jane Russell and Robert Mitchum, he walked away with the film. He was equally funny as the tycoon Burnbridge Waters in “Champagne for Caesar”, co-starring Ronald Colman (1950), one of his favorite roles. The actor’s first major horror film was “House of Wax” (1953) in which he played a sculptor driven to become a serial killer. He commanded the screen, largely because his horror villains were as tragic as they were frightening, and often elicited sympathy. The actor’s next movies were “The Mad Magician” (1954), and the iconic sci-fi film “The Fly” (1958). The following year, Price starred in the “House on Haunted Hill” and the hugely entertaining “The Tingler”. The actor had always been fascinated by Edgar Allen Poe, and had a number of huge successes in Poe adaptations, starting with “The House of Usher” (1960), which earned over $2 million at the US box office, followed by “The Pit and the Pendulum” (1961), “Tales of Terror” (1962), “The Comedy of Terrors” (1963), “The Raven” (1963), and “The Masque of the Red Death” (1964). He also played the lead in “The Last Man on Earth” (1964), the first adaptation of the Richard Matheson novel “I Am Legend”. A year later, Price gave a chilling performance as witch hunter Matthew Hopkins in “Witchfinder General”, (1968), set during the English Civil War. He also starred in the comedies “Dr. Goldfoot” and “The Bikini Machine” (1965). The actor reduced his film appearances in the ‘70s, and in 1977, he began playing Oscar Wilde in a one-man stage play. His daughter, Victoria Price, said it was his finest piece of acting. Deliciously childlike, he was a lifelong fan of roller coasters, and narrated a documentary about their history. His last film role was as the inventor in Tim Burton's “Edward Scissorhands” (1990). Price also spent time working as an art consultant for Sears, Roebuck and Co. From 1962 to 1971, Sears offered the "Vincent Price Collection of Fine Art", selling about 50,000 prints to the general public. At home, he was a gourmet cook, and wrote several cookbooks with his second wife, Mary. Price promoted these on talk shows, one of the most famous instances being the November 21, 1975, broadcast of “The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson”, when he demonstrated how to poach a fish in a dishwasher. Politically, he became so liberal that, according to his daughter, "one of my brother's earliest memories is when Franklin Roosevelt's death was announced, and my father fell backward off the sofa sobbing." The actor was also one of the first celebrities to film a public service announcement to help allay fears about AIDS. (In a 2015 interview, Victoria said that her father had had several relationships with men.) The incomparable Vincent Price died in 1993, aged 82.

Being unemployed is mentally exhausting.

You wake up every day trying to stay hopeful, apply to hundreds of jobs, and still end up hearing nothing. Not even a rejection email.

Over time, the silence starts making you question your own worth.

That's why I believe we need to be kinder to people looking for jobs.

If someone reaches out to you for help, at least try to respond. You might not have a job to offer them, and that's okay. Sometimes, even a little guidance or a simple reply can make a difference.

You don't have to help everyone. You don't owe anyone a referral.

But if you can help someone without expecting anything in return, please do.

text:
The ballot is not a mere administrative tally. It is the sacramental expression of a people, the covenantal seal of a sovereign nation, and the direct translation of blood, and history into political power. A regime that permits foreign interlopers to cast ballots has severed its own legitimacy. The ongoing collision between federal authority and the regime in California exposes the rotten core of the managerial state.

More than twenty thousand likely non-citizens occupy the voter rolls of the Golden State. They received mail-in ballots courtesy of a statutory machine designed for one explicit purpose: the permanent dilution of the historic American electorate. The Department of Justice moves to arrest this administrative treason, demanding that unverified foreign votes remain sequestered. The managerial custodians of California scream in resistance, invoking federalism only when it serves their subversion.

We observe a stark diagnostic breakdown of factions in this war for national character.

First, we face the managerial oligarchy. These bureaucrats operate from glass towers, worship procedural neutrality, and despise the concept of a distinct national identity. They treat citizenship as a bureaucratic fiction, a mere administrative tag interchangeable with any global citizen. Their goal is the perpetual pacification of the native population through demographic replacement, and institutional decay.

Second, we confront the auxiliary class of unassimilated proxies. These are the individuals imported by design to serve as demographic ballast for a failing party apparatus. They hold no loyalty to the hearth, the faith, and the history of this land. They function as instruments of dissolution, deployed to shatter the cultural homogeneity required for a free republic to endure.

Third, we represent the traditionalist vanguard. We reject the poison of egalitarian leveling, democratic apathy, and liberal abstraction. We recognize that a nation is a biological and spiritual continuity, not a boarding house for transient economic units. We demand absolute sovereignty, total border security, and the complete purging of the voter rolls.

The struggle over California is not a procedural dispute. It is an existential war for the character of the nation. When a state government willfully shields foreign voters from scrutiny, it commits an act of domestic warfare against the citizenry. The managerial consensus relies on opacity, confusion, and passive surrender. We offer neither.

The administrative machine must bend to the unyielding weight of truth. We reject compromise, moderation, and institutional cowardice. The nation belongs to those who built it, defended it, and bled for it. Restore the boundaries, purge the rolls, and reclaim the sovereign hearth.

text:
🇿🇦⚖️ Sjoe! The Constitution Holds the Line — But the Digital Pipes Still Leak! 🚰📱 ~ 🚰💰 South Africa Supplies the Views — So Where’s the Pay Cheque? 📱🇿🇦 ~ 🤖📲 The Future Is Already on Your Phone — Why Is Opportunity Still Buffering? ⏳🇿🇦
South Africa’s Constitution still does exactly what it was written to do. Section 16 protects the freedom to receive and impart information or ideas, limited only by three narrow exclusions. Section 20 states that no citizen may be deprived of citizenship. 

When parliamentary remarks in early October 2026 tested the edges of those protections, the text itself pulled the conversation back to evidence and process. 

That quiet institutional insistence is not a weakness. It is the load-bearing floor on which any workable sequence for youth opportunity must stand.

The same country that keeps this floor intact records 47.4 percent unemployment among people aged 15 to 34 (Statistics South Africa, 2026). The simplest digital earnings channel—primary view-based payments on the platform that dominates short-form attention—remains closed to accounts registered here. 

Roughly half the public institutions that were supposed to be connected under spectrum obligations are still offline. The last census undercounted the population by approximately 31 percent. And yet commercial satellite distribution models and everyday artificial-intelligence tools already function inside the rules we have.

The claim is therefore precise and testable: the institutional sequence that most effectively expands both formal speech protections and practical digital earnings for the unemployed youth cohort, while remaining inside the existing constitutional text, begins with accurate measurement and basic service delivery, moves through diffusion of tools that already work, and only then presses platforms and regulators for the residual openings. 

Everything else is theatre that the Constitution itself refuses to stage.

1. The Floor That Still Holds

Section 16(1) of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996, is not a suggestion. It guarantees the freedom to receive or impart information or ideas. Subsection (2) lists the only three exclusions that survive judicial scrutiny: propaganda for war, incitement of imminent violence, and advocacy of hatred based on race, ethnicity, gender or religion that constitutes incitement to cause harm. 

Section 20 is categorical: no citizen may be deprived of citizenship. When a parliamentary committee exploring the foreign-policy consequences of domestic advocacy appeared to test those boundaries, the subsequent official clarification returned immediately to the text and to recent Constitutional Court authority.

Even a broader paraphrase of the limitation clause was publicly corrected against the actual wording. The practical effect is institutional rather than rhetorical. Expansive claims about unprotected speech or conditional citizenship are forced onto the terrain of evidence, formal process and judicial scrutiny. 

Oversight is not frozen; it is required to justify itself under the limitations clause. The 1996 text, written against the memory of conditional citizenship and state censorship, continues to operate as a live constraint. 

Any credible path to digital opportunity for youth must begin by recognising that this floor is still load-bearing.

What makes the floor especially resilient is its origin. The negotiators of the mid-1990s had lived through decades in which political loyalty could determine legal status. They therefore designed a Bill of Rights that treats citizenship and expression as prior to the preferences of any temporary majority. 

That design choice still shapes daily institutional behaviour. 

When political language drifts toward expansive interpretations, the text itself reasserts the narrower boundary. The result is not paralysis. It is a requirement that any restriction survive a demanding justification test. 

In comparative terms, few post-authoritarian constitutions have maintained such consistent textual resistance to informal expansion of speech limitations.

Sjoe!
Thirty years later the Constitution is still doing the quiet work of saying “show me the clause” while the rest of the room argues about the mood of the moment.

Stirring Questions:
How far may a state treat the foreign reception of domestic advocacy as a harm the speakers must answer for without expanding the three exclusions in Section 16(2)?
What measurable standard would determine when advocacy crosses from protected political speech into conduct that Parliament may examine under its oversight powers?
Why does the public availability of the actual constitutional text matter more than any official paraphrase of it?

What these questions together reveal:
They expose the difference between a living constitutional constraint and political weather. Taken together they ask whether South Africa will continue to treat the 1996 text as a hard boundary or allow it to become a soft suggestion. The answer determines whether speech remains a reliable tool for demanding digital opportunity or becomes conditional on institutional comfort.

2. The Closed Tap

As of October 2026 the primary Creator Rewards programme on the dominant short-form platform—the mechanism that converts qualified views into direct payments—remained unavailable to accounts registered in South Africa. Government ministers had raised the exclusion repeatedly. 

Secondary routes (LIVE gifts and the brand-deal marketplace launched in September 2026) existed, yet they imposed higher thresholds and extra steps. For a cohort facing 47.4 percent unemployment among those aged 15 to 34 in the second quarter of 2026, the simplest automatic conversion of attention into household income stayed geographically filtered. 

South African content continued to generate advertising value that largely did not return to the households producing it. Other platforms already offered primary monetisation pathways, demonstrating that the exclusion is a design choice rather than a technical necessity.

The pipes of speech are open. The pipes of earnings are not. The asymmetry is structural: value is created inside the country and captured outside it. Economically this is a classic case of incomplete reciprocity. Attention is a scarce resource. When a platform extracts that resource from one jurisdiction while restricting the primary payment mechanism that would return value to the same jurisdiction, it creates a silent transfer. 

Secondary tools mitigate the transfer but do not reverse it. The result is a digital economy in which young South Africans can generate the raw material of the attention market yet remain largely excluded from its simplest form of compensation.

International comparisons sharpen the point. Several jurisdictions with lower youth unemployment rates and smaller creative sectors already enjoy the primary payment channel. The barrier is therefore not technological capacity or market size. 

It is a platform decision about geographic eligibility that has so far resisted sustained public pressure.

Sjoe!
We are free to speak, free to create, free to generate the views that fund the global machine—and still waiting for the machine to notice that the creators live here too.

Stirring Questions:
What justifies a permanent geographic barrier between attention generated in one jurisdiction and the primary payment mechanism for that attention?
How long can secondary tools be presented as adequate substitutes for the simplest form of reciprocal payment?
When other platforms already pay South African creators, what exact public-interest harm is prevented by maintaining the closed primary channel on the dominant short-form platform?

What these questions together reveal:
They shift the conversation from gratitude for secondary tools to the institutional logic of the primary exclusion. Collectively they ask whether platform design choices that systematically disadvantage one country’s young creators can remain outside the scope of serious public policy while speech about those choices remains fully protected.

3. The Foundational Leak

Under spectrum-licence obligations attached to the 2022 auction, mobile operators were required to connect 21 878 public service institutions. By March 2026 only 10 851—approximately 49 percent—had been connected. Only three of the five operators met the interim 65 percent threshold for their individual targets (Portfolio Committee on Communications and Digital Technologies, 2026). 

Data costs continued to force rationing. Power interruptions disrupted both content creation and skills acquisition. Tens of thousands of ICT vacancies sat unfilled while millions of young people remained outside the labour market.

Expanding platform access or announcing new skills programmes produces limited results when the everyday infrastructure required for sustained online presence is incomplete. Cheaper data, reliable power, completed institutional connectivity and practical digital literacy are not peripheral administrative issues. 

They are the binding first constraint. Fixing them multiplies the return on every subsequent intervention.

The leak has a longer history. Spectrum was allocated with explicit public-interest conditions precisely because high-demand frequencies are a scarce public resource. When the public side of the bargain lags, the private value of the spectrum is fully realised while the social value remains partial. 

The result is a quiet subsidy running in the wrong direction: the public provides the scarce resource, the operators capture the commercial upside, and the institutions that were supposed to receive connectivity wait. 

Political science has a dry name for this pattern—incomplete contracting under weak enforcement—but the lived experience is simpler. 

Young people cannot create content or acquire skills on networks that do not reach the places where they study and work.

Sjoe!
We auctioned the airwaves with fine print about schools and clinics. The fine print appears to have been written in disappearing ink.

Stirring Questions:
If spectrum obligations were accepted as the price of high-demand licences, what institutional mechanism now enforces the public side of that bargain at the required pace?
How many of the 47.4 percent unemployed youth are currently locked out of digital opportunity by the simple absence of reliable connectivity and affordable data rather than by any lack of aptitude?
When skills programmes and platform pressure are announced against a backdrop of incomplete basic infrastructure, whose long-term interest is being optimised?

What these questions together reveal:
They relocate the problem from individual motivation to institutional delivery. Together they ask whether South Africa will continue to treat connectivity as an optional extra or finally recognise it as the precondition for every digital opportunity it claims to want for its young people.

4. The Uncounted Denominator

The 2022 census recorded a net undercount of approximately 31 percent—the highest figure published by the United Nations Population Division for any census with a reported undercount (Moultrie & Dorrington, 2024). 

Subsequent mid-year population estimates continued to carry that legacy. Every means-tested grant, clinic allocation, school place and skills programme therefore operated against an uncertain denominator. Planning against an incomplete headcount turns constitutional socio-economic obligations into exercises in approximation and reduces the efficiency of scarce public resources.

Accurate, publicly trusted continuous population registers would improve allocation efficiency, lower the political temperature around small countable groups, and allow youth programmes to be designed with greater precision. Until the measurement deficit is closed, downstream interventions—including those aimed at digital earnings—remain blunt instruments regardless of the quality of their design.

Measurement failures have compounding effects. When the state does not know how many people live in a given area, every subsequent decision—where to place a clinic, how many teachers to deploy, which skills programmes to fund—begins with an error term. That error term is not neutral. It systematically disadvantages the least visible and the most mobile. 

In a country with high internal migration and large informal settlements, an incomplete count becomes a structural barrier to targeted opportunity. The constitutional promise of progressive realisation of socio-economic rights is harder to keep when the population itself remains only partially known.

Sjoe!
We are trying to design precision programmes with a ruler that still thinks the country is 31 percent smaller than it is. The programmes are not the only thing that ends up approximate.

Stirring Questions:
What single institutional step would most reduce the political and administrative friction around grants, skills programmes and digital access?
How would public confidence change if the national population figure were settled and independently verifiable?
Why does the absence of a continuous register continue to shape both fiscal risk and the targeting of opportunity for the unemployed youth cohort?

What these questions together reveal:
They identify measurement as a governance prerequisite rather than a technical detail. Collectively they ask whether South Africa will continue to plan against an uncertain headcount or finally treat accurate population data as infrastructure as essential as electricity or spectrum.

5. The Pathways Already Inside the Frame

Local-distributor satellite models—Amazon Leo through the already-licensed operator Herotel—advanced toward commercial residential and business service targeted for 2027 without requiring amendment of the 2005 Electronic Communications Act’s ownership provisions. 

Everyday generative artificial intelligence already resided on millions of existing smartphones. Across decades of labour-market evidence, complementary technologies have expanded rather than destroyed most occupations once ordinary people could use the tools; pure occupational extinction has been vanishingly rare. 

Micro-credentials and informal adoption moved faster than formal recognition frameworks.

Waiting for perfect new legislation is therefore not the only available strategy. Commercial routes that accept existing architecture, combined with rapid practical literacy on devices already in circulation, can deliver usable connectivity and productivity gains more quickly than comprehensive statutory reform. 

The highest-return near-term sequence is to accelerate diffusion of the tools and pathways that already function inside the current legal and technological frame.

The deeper insight is about institutional sequencing. When a country possesses both a strong constitutional floor and incomplete basic infrastructure, the rational order of operations is not to begin with the most contested legislative changes. It is to complete the uncontested foundations and diffuse the tools that already fit the existing rules. 

Satellite distribution through local licensees, practical AI literacy on devices people already own, and micro-credentials that signal competence faster than formal qualifications are all available inside the present legal frame. 

Using them first creates the material conditions in which later, more contested reforms become both more feasible and more legitimate.

Sjoe!
Sometimes the most radical path is the one that does not require rewriting the rulebook before the first step can be taken.

Stirring Questions:
If a local-distributor model can deliver the same category of satellite service without amending the Act, what additional public value would a pure-foreign licence create that justifies continued legislative blockage?
When generative AI already sits on millions of phones, what formal recognition barrier still prevents the productivity gains from reaching the unemployed youth cohort at scale?
Why does the historical pattern of complementary technologies expanding work remain less visible in public debate than the rare cases of pure occupational extinction?

What these questions together reveal:
They test the preference for new legislation over existing capacity. Together they ask whether South Africa will continue to treat the absence of ideal rules as a reason to delay usable progress, or finally treat usable progress as the strongest argument for later rule refinement.

Synthesis

The five strands form a single, testable argument. 
The constitutional floor is strong enough to protect the speech required to demand change. 
The primary earnings tap is still closed. 
The service-delivery pipes leak. 
The population denominator remains uncertain. 
Yet commercial and technological pathways already function inside current statutes.

The institutional sequence that most effectively expands both formal speech protections and practical digital earnings for the unemployed youth cohort, while remaining inside the existing constitutional text, is therefore sequential and cumulative:
Settle the population count and complete basic service-delivery obligations so that targeting and access become possible.

Accelerate diffusion of tools and commercial pathways (satellite distribution models, everyday AI literacy, micro-credentials) that already function inside current rules.

Use the protected space of Section 16 speech to press platforms for primary monetisation access and regulators for the residual legislative adjustments that remain necessary.

The argument is falsifiable. A transparent continuous population register that commands public confidence, measurable completion of the spectrum connectivity obligations, rapid diffusion of practical AI literacy with recognised micro-credentials, and the opening of primary view-based payments on the dominant short-form platform would each require revision of the diagnosis if they failed to improve youth earnings and participation. 

Persistence of the current pattern strengthens it.

Independent lines of evidence—from constitutional text, labour-force statistics, spectrum compliance data, census quality assessments and platform eligibility rules—converge on the same sequence. 

The floor is solid. The leaks are measurable. The closed tap is a design choice. The pathways already exist. The order of operations is therefore not a matter of preference. It is a matter of institutional realism.

Sjoe!
The Constitution held the line. The pipes still leak. The taps remain half-closed. And yet the path is already visible to anyone willing to walk it without first demanding a new map.

Objections

Some will argue that ownership and security rules remain essential and that any diffusion risks irreversible loss of control. The evidence does not require abandoning those goals; it requires distinguishing the original public purpose from the practical effect of rigid application on technologies that did not exist when the rules were written.

Others will claim the delays are ordinary regulatory caution. The documentary record shows a clear statutory floor, an explicit regulatory finding that only legislation can alter it, and a parallel connectivity shortfall of more than 50 percent against accepted licence obligations.

A third objection holds that secondary tools and political pressure are already sufficient. The persistence of the primary earnings exclusion, the 47.4 percent youth unemployment rate, and the incomplete institutional connectivity demonstrate that secondary mechanisms have not closed the gap for ordinary young creators.

Conclusion

South Africa already possesses the constitutional text strong enough to protect the speech required to demand digital opportunity, the commercial models that can deliver connectivity without new statutes, and the everyday tools that historically expand work when diffusion is broad. 

What remains is the institutional sequence that treats measurement and service delivery as prerequisites, accelerates the pathways already inside the frame, and only then presses for the residual openings. 

The floor still holds. The pipes can be repaired. The taps can be opened. The pathway is already visible to anyone willing to walk it without first rewriting the rules that keep the walking legitimate.

The converging evidence proves that the highest-return sequence for expanding both formal speech protections and practical digital earnings for South Africa’s unemployed youth cohort, while remaining inside the existing constitutional text, begins with accurate counting and completed basic infrastructure, proceeds through diffusion of tools that already function, and only then presses platforms and regulators for primary access.

text:
Useful, informative eye-opener & easy to read, even though written mainly for British readership: 

These poisonous lies about Zionism need to die

Israel is a multiethnic democracy and the Jewish connection to the Holy Land reaches back millennia
Adam LeBor 

Walking along the Pilgrimage Road from the Pool of Siloam to the base of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem is a kind of time travel. Built around 2,000 years ago, its precisely engineered stone paving has recently been restored and the road opened to the public. Roman legionnaires ran amok here in 70AD, burning the shops and houses and slaughtering the Jewish rebels. A layer of ash is still embedded in the walls.

If only it were possible for Israel to arrange a trip for Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens – and for the 1,022 party members who voted for a motion (which Polanski didn’t turn up to vote for) declaring that Zionism supports an “ethnonationalist Jewish state” based on the “exclusion and/or domination” of non-Jews, while Israel must effectively be replaced by a “democratic Palestinian state”. The lie that Zionism is racism has long outlived its Soviet creators. Zionism is the movement to establish a democratic, non-exclusive Jewish state in the historic homeland of the Jewish people.

Do the Greens know that 21 per cent of Israel’s 10.3 million population are Muslim, Christian and Druze Arabs? These minorities in Israel are diplomats, judges on the supreme court, members of the Knesset, military officers, doctors, lawyers, businessmen and women, part of a thriving professional middle class. Sometimes they suffer discrimination. Modern Israel, like every democracy, is a work in progress. But the overwhelming majority of Israeli-Arabs would live nowhere else.

Nor is Zionism a “settler-colonial” ideology. In truth, the Jewish connection to Israel reaches back millennia to the time of Abraham. Jewish kings and dynasties exercised centuries of intermittent sovereignty from the Davidic era, around 3,000 years ago, until 70AD. Even after Titus’s soldiers destroyed the Temple the Jews rose again against the Romans, in 132AD, before being exiled. The Jewish connection to the Holy Land continued through religious and spiritual Zionism.

The father of modern Zionism was Theodor Herzl, an Austro-Hungarian journalist and the author of The Jewish State, published in 1896. Herzl argued that, despite the new legal protections given to Jews by modern European states, deep-rooted anti-Semitism meant they had no future in Europe. He was correct, as later events proved.

Modern Zionism was not an outlier, but one of many modern anti-colonial movements pressuring the creaking Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian empires to grant freedom to their subject peoples. Another was the emergence of Arab, and later, Palestinian nationalism – the latter partly as a response to Zionism. Palestinian leaders then – unlike their counterparts nowadays – acknowledged the historic Jewish connection to the Holy Land, although they completely rejected the idea of Jewish sovereignty.

Zionism, like socialism, has many currents. Some Zionists even believe in a bi-national Jewish-Arab state. Nowadays a minority of extremists want to see the Palestinians expelled and Biblical-style Jewish sovereignty restored. Neither of them is intrinsic to the ideology. Tony Blair and Josef Stalin were both socialists, but otherwise had nothing in common. 

Interviewed by the BBC, Polanski sought to square the circle. The motion would stand for two years, he said, although ultimately he would like to amend it. “I want to move away from one state, towards saying that Israelis and Palestinians should decide their future for themselves.” Israelis and Palestinians have decided their own futures for decades.

In November 1947, the UN passed Resolution 181. It proposed dividing Palestine, then under British rule, into independent Jewish and Arab states, linked through economic union. The Yishuv, the Zionist leadership, accepted it. The Palestinians did not. The previous month Abdul Rahman Hassan Azzam Pasha, secretary-general of the Arab League, had declared that a Jewish state would lead to “a war of extermination and momentous massacre which will be spoken of like the Mongolian massacre and the Crusades”.

In May 1948, five Arab armies invaded. There was no war of extermination. Instead Israel, fighting for its life, won. Around 700,000 Palestinians fled, an event known as “the Nakba”, or catastrophe. The picture is complex. Some departed before the war, some were encouraged to leave by Arab leaders and some were expelled by Israeli troops. Many simply took flight in the terror and chaos.

In Jaffa, the Arab mayor, Yousef Heikal, encouraged his fellow Arabs to leave – much of the middle class had already departed months earlier. In Haifa, the Jewish mayor, Shabtai Levy, pleaded with local Arabs not to leave. Wars and collapsing empires – and their aftermath – have produced misery and refugees for millennia.

The case of Israel/Palestine is not unique. The numbers involved are a fraction of the catastrophic consequences of, for example, the 1947 partition of India and Pakistan: millions were displaced amid widespread massacres and mass rape. Across eastern Europe, millions of ethnic Germans were expelled or fled after 1945.

The 1923 Treaty of Lausanne ordered the transfer of more than one million ethnic Greeks from their centuries-old homeland in what became the new Turkish state, and the expulsion of hundreds of thousands of Muslims from Greece to Turkey. There is no talk among Greens of the “ethnonationalist” Greek or Turkish states, even though they were specifically created as such by an international treaty.

In July 1995, the Bosnian Serb army committed genocide at Srebrenica, murdering more than 8,300 Muslim men and boys. The Bosnian Serb entity remains a recognised, functioning part of Bosnia Herzegovina, ignored by the progressive gaze.

The early 1990s Oslo Accords gave the Palestinians limited self-government. In response Yassir Arafat launched the Second Intifada of suicide bombings. A series of negotiations followed in the early 2000s under American leadership which broadly offered the Palestinians around 95 per cent of the West Bank. The Palestinians rejected every proposal.

In 2025 Israel withdrew from Gaza. The following year the Hamas terrorist movement won legislative elections in the West Bank and Gaza. There it set up a quasi-Palestinian state. Billions of dollars of aid was channelled into building up an army and tunnel network hundreds of miles long. On October 7 2023, Hamas carried out the worst mass slaughter of Jews since the Holocaust, and killed any likelihood of a Palestinian state.

Offered numerous opportunities for peace and statehood, the Palestinians have refused every one. Instead they – and Hamas – have been rewarded by western countries, including the UK, with recognition of a ghost state that does not exist.

Earlier this month, Mahmoud Abbas, the 90-year-old president of the Palestinian Authority, postponed elections again – this time until 2027. There have been none since 2006. Perhaps one day the Palestinians will be given the opportunity to vote for a leadership that wants to live alongside Israel in peace and security – and the Greens will reconnect with reality.

text:
Franco made the Führer wait.

October 23, 1940, Hendaye station. Hitler’s train sat on the Spanish-French border while Franco’s was still rolling. 

When the Caudillo finally arrived, the most powerful man in Europe had already been left cooling his heels. The meeting that followed dragged on for nine hours of circular demands, territorial shopping lists, & polite obstruction. 

Hitler wanted Spain in the war, Gibraltar, the Mediterranean, a southern flank against Britain. Franco wanted grain, oil, French North Africa, & time. He got the last of those.

On paper Franco was prepared to honor the war. He had accepted Axis aid during the Civil War, shared anti-communist rhetoric, & kept the door open. In practice he treated the alliance as a transaction he had no intention of completing on Hitler’s terms. 

Spain was exhausted, its army thin, its ports vulnerable. Joining would have been suicide dressed as gratitude.

What made the stall personal, not merely strategic, was the deeper contempt. Franco was a devout Catholic who had built his regime on the Church. 

Hitler’s private remarks about Christianity, his open scorn for its “Jewish” origins, its universalism, its refusal to kneel to race, were known in Madrid. 

Franco had no interest in subordinating Catholic Spain to a movement that treated the faith as an obstacle or a temporary tool. 

The waiting, the endless conditions, the refusal to commit: these were not only military prudence. They were the behavior of a man who disliked the person across the table & saw no reason to hurry into his war.

Hitler left furious. He later said he would rather have several teeth pulled than negotiate with Franco again. Spain stayed out. Gibraltar stayed British. 

The meeting at Hendaye remains one of the cleaner examples of a weaker power using delay, faith, & national interest to refuse a stronger one, without ever quite saying no.
